content.p: For years the Gilgo Beach killings were among New York's most perplexing unsolved cases. Skeletal remains had turned up along a barrier-island parkway on Long Island, and the story became the subject of a bestselling book, a Netflix movie and true-crime documentaries. On 8 April 2026 the man charged with the crimes, Rex Heuermann, a Manhattan architect who lived in the suburb of Massapequa Park, stood in a Suffolk County courtroom and pleaded guilty to seven murders. He also admitted to an eighth killing, that of Karen Vergata, for which he had never been charged.

On 17 June 2026 Justice Timothy Mazzei sentenced him to life in prison without the possibility of parole. The hearing ended a case that had begun with a body found by two hunters in 1993 and had taken more than three decades to resolve.
content.h2: A search that found other bodies
content.p: The public part of the case began on 1 May 2010, when Shannan Gilbert, a sex worker, disappeared from the barrier-island community of Oak Beach. According to NBC News, she placed a 911 call from a client's home in Oak Beach, then knocked on a neighbour's door and ran away down the street. Police later said Gilbert most likely drowned by accident, and investigators did not link her death to the other killings.

On 11 December 2010 a police officer training a dog along Ocean Parkway found human remains. Police first thought they might have found Gilbert. The remains were those of Melissa Barthelemy. Two days later investigators found three more sets of remains, belonging to Maureen Brainard-Barnes, Megan Waterman and Amber Lynn Costello. All four women had been wrapped in burlap. They were young, they had worked as escorts, and, CNN reported, they had advertised on Craigslist. They became known as the "Gilgo Four". On 14 December 2010 the Suffolk County police commissioner, Richard Dormer, said publicly that a serial killer might be responsible.

Searches soon turned up many more remains. By April 2011, according to ABC7 New York's timeline, investigators had found ten sets of remains, and by May officials said they might be looking for three or four killers. Gilbert's own remains were found in a tidal marsh near Oak Beach in December 2011. NBC New York noted that her family still suspected she had been killed.

The investigation then stalled. Some families of the victims complained that detectives did not treat the cases seriously because of the women's work. Rodney Harrison, the police commissioner in 2023, said that there "might have been some things that we could have done better". In 2015 the county's police chief, James Burke, was arrested in a separate matter; CNN reported that he admitted a civil rights violation and a conspiracy to obstruct justice, and received a 46-month sentence.
The eight women whose killings Heuermann admitted were not all found in one place or one decade.

Sandra Costilla, 28, was a native of Trinidad and Tobago who had been living in New York. Two hunters found her body in a wooded area of North Sea, in the Hamptons, on 20 November 1993. She was the earliest of his victims. ABC News reported that prosecutors linked Heuermann to her through DNA from a hair lifted from her shirt.

Karen Vergata, 34, an escort from Manhattan, was last in contact with her family on 14 February 1996. Her legs and feet were found on Fire Island that April, long before anyone could name her. Her skull was found in 2011 near Tobay Beach. She was identified through genetic genealogy; CNN dates the identification to August 2023, while NBC New York dates it to 2022.

Valerie Mack, 24, a mother from Philadelphia who worked as an escort, last saw her family in Port Republic, New Jersey, in the spring or summer of 2000. ABC News, citing court documents, said a hunter's dog found her remains in woods at Manorville on 19 November 2000. The rest of her was found in April 2011 along Ocean Parkway.
Jessica Taylor, 20, vanished in July 2003. Part of her remains were found at Manorville that month and more near Gilgo Beach in March 2011.

Maureen Brainard-Barnes, 25, of Norwich, Connecticut, was last heard from on 9 July 2007, when she told a friend she was leaving her hotel to meet a client. Melissa Barthelemy, 24, of the Bronx, disappeared in July 2009. Her family later received taunting phone calls from her mobile phone, and one caller told her sister, "You won't. I killed her." Megan Waterman, 22, from Maine, was last seen on 6 June 2010 at a motel in Hauppauge. Amber Lynn Costello, 27, of West Babylon, was last seen on 2 September 2010. A male friend later told investigators that the person he presumed was her client drove a Chevrolet Avalanche.

The turn came in early 2022. In January or February of that year, depending on the outlet, the Suffolk County district attorney's office, state police and the FBI formed a task force to look again at the killings. District Attorney Ray Tierney later said the group stayed deliberately quiet and held no media events, because it wanted the killer to relax. The Heuermann name came up as a possible suspect about a month into the work, he said.

The first link was a vehicle. According to the Associated Press, detectives used a vehicle registration database to connect Heuermann to a pickup truck that a witness had reported when one of the women disappeared in 2010. The truck was a Chevrolet Avalanche, which ABC7 described as sparsely purchased on Long Island. Investigators also examined phone location data, financial records, eyewitness descriptions and computer searches, CNN reported. Cellphone data showed that Heuermann had been in contact with some of the women shortly before they vanished, the Associated Press reported, and his internet history showed a strong interest in the killings.

The decisive physical evidence came from DNA. Surveillance officers followed Heuermann in Manhattan, where he worked, and saw him throw a box of pizza crusts into a street bin. They collected it, and the crime lab matched the DNA to a hair found on burlap used on one of the victims. Because the hairs were old, rootless and degraded, prosecutors also used whole genome sequencing. A filing described by CNN said two forensic laboratories had tied hairs from six of the seven charged victims to Heuermann or to members of his household.

Heuermann was arrested in Manhattan on 13 July 2023 and charged with murdering Barthelemy, Waterman and Costello. His lawyer Michael Brown said he was in tears and said "I didn't do this". Prosecutors added charges over the following seventeen months or so: Brainard-Barnes in January 2024, Costilla and Taylor in June 2024, and Mack in December 2024. After a search of his home in 2024, prosecutors said they had found a "planning document" on his devices, which, according to the bail application, set out a strategy for future killings, including how to avoid apprehension and leaving DNA. In court filings and news conferences they called it a blueprint.
content.h2: The rulings that shaped the plea
content.p: In the pre-trial period two decisions went against the defence. On 3 September 2025 Justice Mazzei ruled that the whole-genome DNA evidence could go before a jury, the first time such evidence had been admitted in a New York court. His 27-page decision, reported by CBS New York, found that the principles behind the method were accepted as reliable in the scientific community. The defence had called the process inaccurate and compared it to "magic". Later that month the judge also refused to split the seven murder counts into separate trials.

After the plea Brown called the DNA ruling "monumental" and said that a single trial on seven killings would have had a heavy cumulative effect on a jury. Tierney said no deal on sentence had been bargained: the office would take a plea whenever Heuermann chose to offer one. He said talk of Vergata came up in a proffer session, a meeting in which a defendant gives information that prosecutors agree not to use against him. After that, Tierney said, a plea began to seem possible.

On 8 April 2026, five months before the trial date, Heuermann stood in a dark suit with his hands shackled behind him and answered the judge and the district attorney. The hearing lasted about thirty minutes. CBS New York reported that the plea covered three counts of first-degree murder and four of second-degree murder. Asked whether he had killed each victim by strangulation, he said yes. He told the court that he contacted several of the women on burner phones and lured them with the offer of money, and that he bound some of them with burlap before leaving their bodies along Ocean Parkway.

The sentence terms were fixed in the agreement: three consecutive terms of life without parole for Barthelemy, Waterman and Costello, followed by four consecutive terms of 25 years to life for the others. He would also face no other prosecution in connection with the eight women, and he was required to cooperate with the FBI, working with its behavioural analysts on catching other serial killers.

Asa Ellerup, Heuermann's former wife, and their daughter sat in the last row. Afterward Ellerup said her thoughts were with the victims' families. Her lawyer, Robert Macedonio, said she and her daughter had no knowledge of or involvement in the crimes, and prosecutors said the family had been away at the time of the killings. Tierney told reporters that Heuermann had "walked among us" as a normal suburban father. Suffolk Police Commissioner Kevin Catalina called him a "sadistic, soulless, murderous monster".

At the sentencing on 17 June 2026, relatives of most of the victims spoke. JoAnn Mack, Valerie Mack's mother, told Heuermann that what he had done was "beyond what words can express". Liliana Waterman, who was three when her mother disappeared, described a world "shattered" in an instant. Amanda Funderburg, Barthelemy's sister, told him he could look at her while she spoke, and recalled a taunting call she received from him when she was 15. Melissa Cann, Brainard-Barnes's sister, said she had carried survivor's guilt for years and that it was "not mine to carry". Ruth Ramos, Costilla's sister, said in a statement read by the district attorney that justice ensured the women were no longer forgotten.

Heuermann, 62, spoke briefly: "There are no words I can say. I am responsible for all that was said in this room." Mazzei asked whether he was sorry for what he had done to the women and called him a coward. Mazzei imposed the agreed sentences, to run consecutively, then ordered court officers to remove him, and relatives applauded. His former wife and children did not attend, their lawyers said, out of respect for the victims' families.
Heuermann had been held in the county jail in Riverhead since 2023 and was due to be moved to a state prison within days. Sheriff Errol Toulon said he spent those years alone in a segregated cell.

Investigators think Heuermann may be linked to further killings, and he has promised to help the FBI. They do not believe, however, that all the remains found on Ocean Parkway came from one killer. NBC New York reported in a timeline that the toddler found there was identified through DNA as the daughter of the woman known as "Peaches", whom police identified in 2025, and that a Florida man, Andrew Dykes, pleaded not guilty in December 2025 to killing them. That case was unconnected to the other Gilgo Beach deaths. The remains of an Asian man found in April 2011, whom investigators put at late teens or early twenties when he died, have never been identified. At the sentencing Tierney would not say whether he thought Heuermann was responsible and said genetic genealogy might be used to give the person "some dignity".
